summary: This informational memo discusses the requirements on how IETF output is published. It starts from the point that technical publication is how specifications are disseminated to the community, so the requirements of the publication process should be understood.

eli5.summary: Writing good rules isn't enough; people have to be able to read them. This lists what a good publishing service for the IETF should do.

questions: what does the ietf technical publisher do
what is the rfc editor responsible for
how long should rfc publication take
subtitle: What the IETF wants from the organization that publishes its technical specifications.

tldr.problem: The IETF's output only helps if it is published well, and the IETF needed a clear statement of what it expects from its technical publisher before writing future contracts.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists 22 publication tasks, such as editing, reference checks, errata and indexing. For each it gives the task, how the IETF handles it today and derived requirements, then adds goals for timeframes and throughput.
tldr.outcome: It records IETF consensus on the publisher's duties and is meant for use in future contracts. It does not judge how well the current publisher, the RFC Editor, meets them.

today: RFC 4714 is an Informational RFC from October 2006. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The IETF discusses, develops and disseminates technical specifications, so published specifications are an important output. The IETF technical publisher handles the final steps of producing them. This memo sets out requirements on the publisher's duties and on how it interacts with the IETF.

It is expected to be used in preparing future contracts. It is not a discussion of how well the current publisher, the RFC Editor, meets the requirements. It also does not debate what counts as an RFC. The task list was derived from the RFC Editor's work and from publishers in other standards bodies including 3GPP, ATIS, ETSI, IEEE and ITU.

Left out of scope are policies on input and output formats, character sets, layout and style, and non-technical sections.
sections.eli5: The IETF writes down what it expects from the people who publish its documents, so it can hire them with clear rules. It is not grading the current publisher.

sections.title: Where Publication Fits
sections.content:
The memo places technical publication in the life of a working group document. The document is created and edited, then goes through reviews (Working Group Last Call, Area Director review, IETF Last Call, IANA review and IESG review). Once the IESG approves it technically, post-approval processing begins, and that is where the technical publisher works.

A document shepherd is an individual designated by the IESG to guide a document through the reviews and publication, and is often not an Area Director.
sections.eli5: A document goes through many rounds of checking first. The publisher steps in at the very end, after everyone has agreed it is ready.

sections.title: The 22 Tasks and Their Requirements
sections.content:
Each task has a description, a discussion of how the IETF handles it, and derived requirements named like Req-POSTEDIT-1. Most use SHOULD. The tasks include pre-approval review, post-approval editing, validation of references and formal languages (ASN.1, ABNF, XML), insertion of IANA parameter values, technical corrections, permanent identifiers, format conversion, status tracking, expedited handling, withdrawal or hold of documents, notification, errata, indexing, access, statistics, help services and liaison.

Some themes recur. The publisher should not perform technical review in the IETF standards stream. Changes after approval must be tracked and signed off, with the Area Director as the authority. The publisher should show restraint with stylistic edits, since readability changes can inadvertently alter consensus wording. In rare cases, text may need to be published verbatim at the IESG's request.

For formats, the publisher should accept ASCII text and publish ASCII text and PDF files. IETF specifications are published only in English. For the archive, the publisher should keep the index and permanent archive and prevent modification by external parties.
sections.eli5: The memo lists 22 jobs, such as fixing spelling, checking that links work, keeping a list of mistakes found later, and keeping every document safe and findable forever. For each job it says what a good publisher should do.

sections.title: Performance Goals
sections.content:
Performance expectations are goals, not requirements, because publication is a process and not all of it is under the publisher's control. Actual targets are to be set in the contract.

The goals are an average publication time of under a month (Goal-TIMEFRAMES-1), pre-approval review in under 10 days (Goal-TIMEFRAMES-2), and no long-term growth in the length of the publication queue (Goal-THROUGHPUT-1). Long publication times cause trouble inside the IETF, since authors move on and tempting post-approval fixes accumulate. They also cause trouble outside, since other organizations cannot cite a document without an RFC number.
sections.eli5: The IETF wants documents published in about a month on average and does not want the waiting line to keep getting longer.

sections.title: Effects on the IETF and Security
sections.content:
Many requirements also imply work for the IETF itself. Examples are deciding who may approve post-approval technical corrections, how identifiers are assigned, how errata are vetted, and how status changes to published documents are communicated to the publisher. The memo expects companion documents to cover these processes.

On security, it warns of a tussle between readability edits and security wording that was carefully negotiated, so extreme caution is needed when changing security text. Processes should prevent unapproved changes, and the archive should be secured against tampering. The IANA section only says new requirements need review by IANA and the IETF.
sections.eli5: Some of these rules mean the IETF has to organize its own side too. And because careful wording about safety is easy to damage, editors must be extra careful there.

references.text: Internet Architecture Board and B. Carpenter, "Charter of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB)", BCP 39, RFC 2850, May 2000.
